strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing an underexplored but practically important task: monocular 3D keypoint estimation without multi-view supervision or manual annotations
Elegant and intuitive technical approach leveraging multi-view diffusion models to provide both geometric supervision and feature extraction
Comprehensive experimental breadth across multiple datasets (Human3.6M, Stanford Dogs, DAVIS, GSO, AP-10K) and scenarios (controlled, in-the-wild, out-of-domain)
Strong generalization demonstrated qualitatively to unseen object categories and domains despite training only on limited data
Thorough ablation studies (Table 2) validating the importance of diffusion features and number of views
Practical versatility: framework extends beyond keypoints to enable animatable 3D object generation
Clear and well-structured presentation with effective visualizations
weaknesses: Modest quantitative improvements on standard benchmarks: 3.79 mm gain over Honari et al. [11] single-view baseline on Human3.6M (85.26 vs 89.05 P-MPJPE); performs 35% worse than multi-view baseline with same keypoint count (85.37 vs 63.0 mm)
Unvalidated generalization claims: Stanford Dogs and AP-10K results are purely qualitative with no ground truth comparisons or quantitative metrics, undermining broad generalization claims

Computational cost not addressed: paper acknowledges multiple denoising steps increase inference cost but provides no runtime comparisons, memory analysis, or practical timing data—critical for real-world applicability
Heavy dependence on pretrained diffusion model quality with limited robustness analysis: no experiments showing failure modes or evaluation with alternative diffusion models

Limited technical novelty: feature aggregation mirrors prior work (Diffusion Hyperfeatures), 3D lifting is standard practice, and self-supervised reconstruction is well-established; primary contribution is combining existing techniques

Incomplete technical documentation: aggregation network training objective unclear, reconstruction network architecture unspecified, adjacency matrix initialization/evolution not discussed, hyperparameter sensitivity unexplored
Evaluation protocol concerns: regressor-based mapping to ground truth assumes semantic alignment of discovered keypoints without validation that points capture meaningful anatomical structure
Unfair baseline comparisons: mixing different keypoint counts (18 vs 32) and comparing single-view method against multi-view methods without adequate modality correction
Scene context limitation fundamentally ignored: object-centric masking approach excludes scene geometry; acknowledged but not addressed experimentally
Missing failure case analysis and systematic breakdown of when/why method fails despite acknowledged limitations

strengths: Timely and interesting application of diffusion models to 3D keypoint discovery; well-motivated use of multi-view priors for monocular estimation
Impressive qualitative generalization to in-the-wild and out-of-domain scenarios across diverse object categories (unseen dog breeds, other animals)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (Human3.6M, Stanford Dogs, DAVIS, GSO, AP-10K) demonstrating breadth
Clear paper presentation with informative figures and logical flow
Additional contribution enabling 3D object manipulation from single images is a useful bonus
weaknesses: Critical: Unfair experimental comparison—KeyDiff3D leverages SV3D, a massive pretrained multi-view diffusion model, while baselines train from scratch; no ablation quantifies the contribution of pretraining vs. the method itself, making performance claims misleading
Overstated 'unsupervised' claim—the method fundamentally depends on SV3D's geometric priors learned from massive supervised data; should be framed as self-supervised leveraging pretrained priors

Limited technical novelty—combines existing techniques (diffusion feature extraction [30], unprojection, reconstruction loss) without significant innovation; main contribution is recognizing diffusion models are useful, which is somewhat incremental

Generalization results lack quantitative validation—all out-of-domain results (DAVIS, GSO, AP-10K) are qualitative only with no error metrics; cannot assess if performance actually remains good on unseen domains vs. merely appearing plausible

Computational efficiency unaddressed—inference requires full denoising (1000 steps) to extract features, acknowledged but not quantified; no runtime comparisons provided despite being critical for practical deployment
Insufficient ablation studies—only two minor ablations; missing sensitivity to timestep τ, number of keypoints N, loss weights λ, and critical ablation isolating SV3D pretraining contribution
Evaluation protocol concerns—regression-based evaluation measures latent space quality rather than direct spatial accuracy; indirect measure that obscures actual performance on the original task

strengths: Novel problem formulation and well-motivated approach: Addresses the underexplored but practical challenge of unsupervised monocular 3D keypoint estimation without requiring calibrated multi-view data or manual annotations.

Clever and elegant solution: Leverages pretrained multi-view diffusion models as geometry-aware feature extractors, effectively transforming implicit 3D priors into explicit 3D features via volumetric unprojection. This represents good knowledge transfer.

Strong and comprehensive empirical results: Outperforms unsupervised single-view baselines on Human3.6M, achieves results competitive with multi-view methods, and demonstrates impressive generalization to in-the-wild (DAVIS) and out-of-domain scenarios (GSO, AP-10K) across diverse categories.

Impressive cross-category generalization: Despite training only on human data (Human3.6M), the method generalizes to animals and non-human objects without category-specific priors, which is a meaningful contribution.

Thorough experimental evaluation: Multiple datasets, both quantitative and qualitative results, sensible ablation studies demonstrating the importance of diffusion features and number of views, and clear visualization of results.

Clear presentation and interpretability: The method is straightforward and well-explained with helpful figures. The pipeline from feature aggregation to 3D volume construction to keypoint extraction is intuitive.
Practical additional application: Beyond keypoints, the method enables 3D object manipulation through skeleton extraction and skinning weights, demonstrating broader utility.
weaknesses: Critical dependence on diffusion model quality: The method is fundamentally bottlenecked by the pretrained diffusion model's ability to generate geometrically consistent views. Failure cases (uncommon poses, occlusions, articulated motion) are acknowledged but not analyzed. This creates a ceiling on improvements and makes the approach less self-contained.

Computational efficiency not analyzed: Inference requires multiple denoising steps to extract intermediate features, likely making the method significantly slower than feed-forward alternatives. No timing comparisons, FLOPs analysis, or inference time measurements provided despite mentioning this as a limitation.

Limited quantitative evaluation on non-human categories: While Human3.6M results are strong, evaluation on Stanford Dogs is largely qualitative, and cross-species generalization (AP-10K, GSO) is entirely qualitative. Claims about generalization would be substantially stronger with quantitative metrics on these datasets.

Evaluation protocol concerns: (1) Uses regression post-processing (linear/MLP) which somewhat masks the quality of unsupervised learning; (2) Procrustes alignment can hide structural errors; (3) Comparison with multi-view methods is not entirely fair—generated views from diffusion may be more consistent than real multi-view data, and the method still generates views at test time.

Insufficient analysis of why the method works: Limited investigation into what 3D feature volumes capture, why diffusion features substantially outperform ResNet features (ablation shows this but doesn't explain), and the connection between object structure and geometric consistency in diffusion priors.

Preprocessing dependency: Requires foreground mask extraction using Grounded SAM, adding a preprocessing dependency on another model. Impact of mask quality on results not explored, and fairness of comparison to methods without this requirement is unclear.
Missing failure case visualization: Limitations section mentions failure modes but doesn't demonstrate them visually. Examples of failure scenarios would strengthen the analysis.

Incomplete ablation and design justification: (1) Why 18 keypoints by default? (2) Why extract features at τ=500? (3) Why M=72 grid resolution? (4) Several hyperparameters lack ablation (e.g., σ and α in skinning weights equation 9 are 'adjustable' but not explored).
Unclear evaluation for animal datasets: How are ground truth 3D keypoints obtained for Stanford Dogs? Standard pose annotation may not exist for this dataset, making validation ambiguous.

Limited novelty in architectural components: The unprojection, volumetric aggregation, and reconstruction are standard techniques. The main contribution is the application to diffusion models, which is valuable but somewhat incremental.

strengths: Novel application of pretrained diffusion models as multi-view priors for unsupervised 3D keypoint learning, elegantly addressing the multi-view supervision problem without manual annotations
Comprehensive evaluation across diverse datasets (Human3.6M, CUB-200-2011, Stanford Dogs, DAVIS, GSO, AP-10K) demonstrating strong generalization to out-of-domain animal categories
Significant quantitative improvements on Human3.6M (MPJPE: 121.34) over unsupervised single-view baselines, with systematic ablation studies validating design choices
Well-motivated technical approach with coherent three-component pipeline (diffusion feature aggregation, 3D lifting, self-supervised training) that is technically sound
Honest discussion of limitations including identified failure modes (left-right ambiguity, diffusion model failures) and acknowledgment of evaluation protocol challenges
Demonstrated practical utility for 3D object manipulation beyond keypoint prediction, showing downstream applicability
weaknesses: Unproven core assumption: lacks theoretical justification and empirical validation that geometric priors from diffusion models (trained on diverse image distributions) align with anatomically/physically correct 3D structures

Fundamental dependence on SV3D diffusion model quality creates an unresolved performance ceiling; no analysis of robustness to diffusion model failures or comparison with alternative multi-view generation approaches

Modest improvements on several benchmarks without statistical significance testing; CUB-200-2011 results are marginal and authors acknowledge difficulty reproducing baseline results with fair evaluation protocols

Evaluation protocol concerns reduce comparison fairness: different preprocessing, different regression setups (linear vs. 2-hidden layer MLP), camera parameter handling not fully specified, and some baseline results cannot be reproduced with official code

Limited novelty in individual technical components: feature aggregation is standard weighted summation, 3D unprojection is basic bilinear sampling, and backbone uses off-the-shelf SV3D—novelty lies primarily in combination

Incomplete computational cost analysis: no training-time overhead comparison despite generating multiple diffusion images per training example; inference comparison (Table 6) lacks baseline comparisons
Unresolved left-right ambiguity limitation (Fig. 8(a)) inherent to monocular methods; while acknowledged, no mitigation strategies proposed

Missing implementation details: camera parameter estimation for SV3D not specified, sensitivity to parameter estimation errors not analyzed, generated image resolution not stated, diffusion timestep selection not justified

strengths: Creative application of multi-view diffusion priors as a source of geometric supervision, enabling unsupervised 3D keypoint discovery without manual 3D annotations

Comprehensive experimental validation across diverse object categories (humans, birds, dogs, generic objects) with detailed ablation studies examining key components (diffusion timesteps, viewpoint count, view aggregation, training data size)
Solid empirical results: competitive or superior performance compared to unsupervised baselines on Human3.6M (121.34 MPJPE) and reasonable cross-category generalization
Practical demonstrations of both keypoint estimation and 3D object manipulation applications
Thorough ablations (Tables 3-5) providing insights into design choices and their impact
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily an engineering contribution combining existing techniques (diffusion models, feature aggregation, standard 3D unprojection). Individual components are standard; the novelty lies mainly in their combination

Insufficient theoretical justification: lacks rigorous explanation for why diffusion-generated views encode useful 3D geometric priors. No analysis of what intermediate 3D feature volumes learn or which geometric properties diffusion models exploit

Fundamental limitations inadequately addressed: (1) left-right ambiguity from monocular input is unresolved with ad-hoc solutions (Figure 8a); (2) entire method ceiling bounded by diffusion model quality with minimal failure mode analysis; (3) computational cost concerns not thoroughly analyzed despite requiring 21 generated views

Evaluation protocol concerns: CUB-200-2011 uses modified protocol due to preprocessing inconsistencies (Appendix A) hampering direct comparison; many baseline results are 'reproduced' rather than original papers' numbers; relies on 2D keypoint annotations as proxy for 3D quality; qualitative-only evaluation on out-of-domain datasets (DAVIS, GSO)

Misleading 'unsupervised' framing: method leverages extensive pretrained 3D-aware diffusion models and uses existing 3D annotations for evaluation (Human3.6M, CUB). True contribution is avoiding manual dataset labeling, not avoiding 3D information

Incomplete comparative analysis: missing comparisons with recent 2024-2025 methods; no evaluation against other approaches using foundation models or diffusion-based features; some baselines from 2019-2021

Technical assumptions not rigorously validated: assumes generated views share canonical coordinate system (Eq. 2-3) without verification; Gaussian line edge detection parameters require justification; 3D feature volume resolution (72³) not ablated

Generalization limitations: testing on similar distributions (mammals/birds within same visual domain); AP-10K results show significant degradation; GSO out-of-domain results visibly lower quality; true generalization across visually distinct domains unclear

Presentation and reproducibility issues: dense method combining many components reduces clarity; key implementation details (Sections D.2-D.3) relegated to appendix; no code release mentioned; dependency on specific proprietary model versions (SV3D-p); no runtime benchmarking in seconds

Minimal failure case analysis: Figure 8 shows failures but lacks systematic taxonomy; limited discussion of when/why method fails; missing sensitivity studies on diffusion model choice and robustness to image quality variations

strengths: Novel approach leveraging pretrained multi-view diffusion models as geometric priors for unsupervised 3D keypoint discovery, with clear motivation and technical soundness
Comprehensive experimental validation across diverse datasets (Human3.6M, CUB-200-2011, Stanford Dogs, DAVIS, GSO, AP-10K) and object categories with both in-domain and out-of-domain evaluation
Solid empirical results demonstrating competitive performance with good generalization to in-the-wild scenarios and challenging occlusions
Technically well-designed pipeline with differentiable operations throughout, enabling end-to-end training without 3D annotations
Extensive ablation studies systematically examining design choices (number of keypoints, diffusion timesteps, training data, view aggregation) with clear insights
Significant practical value enabling scalable 3D keypoint discovery across diverse object categories without expensive manual annotations
Clear presentation with effective figures and well-organized appendices containing detailed implementation information
weaknesses: Absolute performance on 3D tasks shows room for improvement; quantitative validation on some datasets relies on 2D projections without true 3D ground truth (CUB-200-2011, Stanford Dogs), limiting direct validation
Computational efficiency concerns: inference time of ~4.93 seconds per image is relatively slow for practical applications; no computational cost comparison with baselines provided
Strong dependency on specific pretrained diffusion models (SV3D) with limited exploration of performance sensitivity or applicability to domains lacking suitable pretrained models
Acknowledged but unresolved inherent monocular limitation: left-right ambiguity in 3D estimation with limited discussion of practical impact or solutions
Failure case analysis is relatively brief; systematic failure mode characterization and quantitative failure analysis across datasets would strengthen understanding
Out-of-domain generalization shown qualitatively but with limited quantitative validation of performance degradation under domain shift
No mention of code release despite comprehensive implementation details, which impacts reproducibility and community adoption
